questions.question: What is measurement uncertainty?
choices: A quantified range or dispersion associated with a measurement result
An identifiable copying mistake in the results
Only the smallest digit displayed by the instrument
Proof that the measured value has no information

questions.question: What is a systematic measurement error?
choices: Random variation with no consistent direction
Only a misspelled unit
An error that shifts results consistently or predictably
Every difference between two organisms

questions.question: What is a random measurement error?
choices: A fixed offset repeated every time
Unpredictable variation among repeated measurements
A deliberate change to the data
An exact instrument calibration

questions.question: What is instrument resolution?
choices: The agreement between a reading and a reference value
The spread of repeated readings caused by every possible source
The largest value the instrument can measure
The smallest change the instrument can distinguish

questions.question: What does calibration involve?
choices: Adding decimal places without checking against a reference
Averaging readings without considering a known offset
Comparing or adjusting an instrument using known references
Changing the sample until its reading matches a prediction

questions.question: What is parallax error?
choices: A consistent offset caused by incorrect zeroing
A temperature-dependent change in the object's actual size
The random reaction time when operating a stopwatch
A reading error caused by viewing a scale from an unsuitable angle

questions.question: What does 20.0 ± 0.5 cm communicate in a simplified uncertainty statement?
choices: An exact length of 20.5 cm only
A value of 20.0 cm with stated uncertainty of 0.5 cm
A length that must change every second
An uncertainty of 20.0 cm

questions.question: Why can repeated readings help assess random variation?
choices: They show how measurements scatter
They guarantee removal of a fixed calibration offset
They reveal the exact true value without uncertainty
They automatically increase the instrument's resolution

questions.question: Why does averaging many readings not necessarily remove systematic error?
choices: Any average necessarily removes every kind of error
Systematic errors always switch signs between readings
A consistent offset remains in the average
A fixed offset is canceled by reporting more digits

questions.question: Why are extra unsupported decimal places misleading?
choices: They imply more measurement detail than the method supports
They always improve agreement with a reference
They eliminate limitations of the measuring instrument
The number of written digits determines true accuracy

questions.question: Why should uncertainty be reported with a measurement?
choices: It replaces the need to report a measured value
It proves every reading is an identifiable mistake
It makes every comparison between results impossible
It helps judge comparisons and the result's limitations

questions.question: Why can a stopwatch measurement include observer uncertainty?
choices: Digital stopwatches never have observer effects
Human start and stop reactions affect the recorded time
Reaction time affects only distance, not time readings
All observers react with exactly the same delay

questions.question: Why should a balance be zeroed appropriately before measurement?
choices: Zeroing guarantees all later measurements are exact
An initial offset can bias all readings
Zeroing changes the mass of the object measured
Zeroing increases the instrument's displayed resolution

questions.question: How does relative uncertainty help compare measurements of different sizes?
choices: It records only the absolute uncertainty in the original unit
It measures agreement with a reference instead of a ratio
It always gives identical values for all measurements
It expresses uncertainty as a fraction or percentage of the value

questions.question: Why is uncertainty different from a known blunder such as copying the wrong number?
choices: Uncertainty describes measurement limitations, while the blunder is an identifiable mistake
Both must be ignored in science
Uncertainty means no measurements were made
A blunder always improves precision

questions.question: A length is 50 cm with uncertainty ±1 cm. What is its relative uncertainty?
A balance consistently reads 2 g too high. Which action addresses that problem?
choices: Take more readings without correcting the offset
Report more decimal places
Use a larger sample and ignore the offset
Check and correct its calibration or offset

questions.question: A simplified result is 10.0 ± 0.2 s. Which interval corresponds to that notation?
Two results are 5.0 ± 0.5 cm and 5.2 ± 0.5 cm using comparable uncertainty conventions. What is a cautious interpretation?
choices: They prove different true lengths with certainty
The second object is exactly 0.2 cm longer
The results overlap within their stated uncertainty
Neither result contains a measured value

questions.question: Repeated measurements cluster tightly but a reference check shows a consistent offset. Which description fits?
choices: High precision with systematic bias
Low precision with no systematic bias
Perfect accuracy with zero uncertainty
Random scatter around the correct reference
